pageCache.pageTitle: Our Vision and Values - The Hall School
pageCache.text:
Our Purpose, Values and Ethos
Our Vision
Providing an extraordinary learning journey for every boy.
At The Hall, we inspire a lifelong love of learning and nurture curious minds, generous hearts and a genuine sense of purpose. Through academic ambition, outstanding pastoral care and a breadth of opportunity, boys develop the confidence, values and skills to flourish at school and beyond.
We want every boy to leave The Hall ready for the next stage of his education and equipped to make a positive contribution to the world around him.
Our Aims & Ethos
The Hall provides a high-quality education for boys aged 4 to 13 (Reception to Year 8), enabling every pupil to fulfil his individual potential within a framework of academic ambition, curiosity and care.
We believe children thrive when they feel known, supported and challenged. Alongside academic excellence, we provide a broad and enriching education that encourages boys to think independently, discover their interests and develop confidence in themselves and consideration for others.
The Hall has a Christian foundation and heritage. We warmly welcome boys and families of all faiths and none, fostering an understanding of different religions, beliefs and worldviews within an inclusive and respectful community.
Our school is a happy, nurturing and purposeful community in which every boy is encouraged to contribute positively, take responsibility and make the most of the opportunities available to him. Through strong relationships, expert teaching and a wealth of experiences beyond the classroom, we help pupils grow into thoughtful, capable and well-rounded young people.
These aims are reflected in our values, which guide daily life at The Hall.
Our Values
At The Hall, our values shape everything we do, from how boys learn and grow to how they treat one another and contribute to the community around them. Our four core values are Curiosity, Courage, Community and Kindness.
Together, they underpin our teaching, pastoral care and ambitions for every pupil, creating an environment where boys are challenged, supported and inspired to flourish academically, socially and emotionally.
The result is confident, kind and intellectually curious young people who are well prepared for senior school and for life beyond it.
Curiosity
Questions that lead to understanding
At The Hall, curiosity is where learning begins. From the very earliest years, boys are encouraged to ask questions, explore ideas and think independently. A Year 1 pupil might wonder why an object floats in water and be supported to experiment, predict and explain his thinking. As boys grow, that same curiosity deepens into genuine enquiry – whether questioning how glaciers have shaped Iceland’s landscape while abroad on a geography trip, or digging beneath the surface of a topic to understand how and why things work.Through specialist teaching, stimulating discussion and a wide programme of educational trips and visits, boys learn to think deeply, pursue their interests and develop the intrinsic motivation that underpins both academic excellence and a lifelong love of learning.
Courage
In learning and in lifeCourage at The Hall is about having the confidence to try, even when something feels challenging. In the classroom, academic courage might mean attempting a difficult problem, sharing an original idea, or learning from mistakes. Beyond the classroom, it can often be seen in a performance on stage, whether that’s stepping into spotlight to perform at Cadogan Hall or during a drama production, as well as in everyday moments of social courage, such as being true to oneself or speaking up when something doesn’t feel right. At every age, boys are encouraged to step outside their comfort zones within a safe and supportive environment. By nurturing both intellectual and personal courage, we help boys develop resilience, self‑belief and the confidence to embrace opportunities with integrity and determination.
Community
Stronger togetherCommunity lies at the heart of life at The Hall. From working collaboratively in lessons to contributing through Houses, sports teams, music ensembles and clubs, boys learn that they achieve more as part of something bigger than themselves. Older boys support and mentor younger boys, helping to build a strong sense of belonging and connection across the school. This emphasis on community creates an environment where boys support one another, celebrate shared success and compete with generosity of spirit. It is a culture that balances ambition with kindness, and individual achievement with collective pride. Boys also become part of a community that extends beyond the school grounds. Through partnerships with local schools and charities, initiatives such as our Saturday Club, and an engaged parent and alumni network, boys learn the importance of contributing positively to the world around them. We want every boy to understand that community is something to which we all belong, contribute and take pride.
Kindness
In thought, word and deedKindness shapes how boys experience school every day. It can be seen in the way boys include others in play, encourage one another in rehearsals or support a classmate who is finding something difficult. It is also reflected in the strong relationships between teachers and pupils, where boys are encouraged, challenged and supported with individual care and understanding. As boys mature, kindness grows into empathy, leadership and the confidence to act when something isn’t right. By valuing kindness alongside achievement, we help boys develop emotional intelligence, self‑respect and respect for others. It ensures that ambition is matched with integrity, and that boys grow not only into successful learners, but into thoughtful, compassionate young people.
See our values in action
Discover what life is like at The Hall and how our values shape everyday learning, relationships and opportunities for our boys.Find out how to visit us or attend our next open event.

Head’s Welcome
Welcome to The Hall School
Welcome to The Hall School, one of London’s leading prep schools for boys aged 4 to 13.
A School Where Boys Thrive
The Hall is first and foremost a happy school where boys love to learn. Walk through our doors and you’ll find classrooms buzzing with intellectual curiosity, corridors filled with artwork and achievement, and playing fields where competitive spirit meets genuine camaraderie. Our small class sizes mean every boy is truly known – not just as a pupil, but as an individual with unique talents, interests, and potential.
Our academic results speak for themselves. Hall boys consistently secure places and scholarships at London’s most prestigious senior schools – Westminster, St Paul’s, City of London and University College School among them – as well as leading boarding schools nationwide. One of the greatest benefits of a Hall education is the breadth of pathways available to your son at the time that’s right for them. This success reflects our rigorous curriculum, exceptional teaching, strong personal relationships with senior schools and our commitment to developing independent, confident thinkers.
A Rich Educational Experience
But The Hall offers so much more than exam results. Our investment in specialist facilities and expert teaching means boys benefit from many experiences at a level typically found only at senior schools. Our dedicated off-site sports centre ensures every boy participates regularly across varied disciplines. Our music programme is among London’s finest, with over 80% of boys learning at least one instrument and our annual gala concert at Cadogan Hall a highlight of the school calendar. Drama productions are acclaimed, and our extensive co-curricular offering spans chess to coding, debating to design technology, ensuring every boy discovers passions beyond the classroom.
With three dedicated schools for Junior (ages 4-7), Middle (ages 8-10), and Senior (ages 11-13) boys, we tailor the experience to each developmental stage while fostering a strong sense of whole-school community.
What truly distinguishes The Hall is our ethos. We celebrate ambition and achievement while nurturing kindness and humility. We encourage boys to take risks, ask questions, and think creatively. Our experienced staff know every boy deeply and guide them with wisdom and care. We prepare them not just for senior school entrance exams, but for lives of purpose and contribution.
Whether you are exploring The Hall for the first time or are already part of our community, I invite you to visit and see our school in action. The Hall occupies a special place in the hearts of all who know it – and I think you’ll quickly understand why.
Henry Keighley-Elstub, Head

pageCache.pageTitle: Physical Education and Games - The Hall School
pageCache.text:
Home → School Life → Physical Education and Games
Physical Education and Games
Sport is a cornerstone of life at The Hall. We aim to provide a challenging, enjoyable and rewarding programme that encourages every boy to participate, develop confidence and discover a lifelong love of physical activity.
Our Physical Education and Games curriculum develops not only sporting skills, but also the qualities that help boys thrive both on and off the field. Through sport, boys learn teamwork, resilience, determination, leadership, respect and sportsmanship. We encourage boys to be curious, make decisions independently, embrace challenges and take pride in always doing their best.
Throughout the year, boys enjoy a wide range of sports. In the autumn term, this includes football, rugby, hockey, cross-country and gymnastics, while the summer term brings cricket, tennis and athletics. Alongside lessons, boys can take part in a wide variety of clubs, fixtures and competitions, ensuring opportunities for all abilities and interests.
Sport is also a highlight of the school calendar. We host our own Football Festival, inviting teams from other schools, run an annual Football World Cup competition, organise inclusive House football matches for Years 4–8, host cross-country events on Hampstead Heath, and celebrate dedicated Sports Days for Junior, Middle and Senior School boys. House rounders is another popular summer event.
Junior School boys benefit from our dedicated off-site sports facilities at the Wilf Slack Playing Fields, which provide excellent space for training, fixtures and outdoor activities.
Beyond the curriculum, boys can enjoy a range of exciting sporting experiences, including residential trips, visits to elite sporting venues such as St George’s Park, ski trips for all abilities, opportunities to compete as part of our school ski team, and overseas tours, including cricket tours to Sri Lanka.
Whether a boy is representing the school competitively or simply enjoying being active with friends, our aim is for every pupil to develop confidence, character and a lifelong enthusiasm for sport.

The Music School
There is a vibrant and thriving musical environment at The Hall. The atmosphere of inclusive, purposeful music-making in the school is greatly respected and the majority of boys choose to become involved in the wider musical life of the school as well as within weekly class lessons.
Instrumental and vocal tuition is first class, delivered by visiting professionals and there is a comprehensive programme of ensembles that supports curriculum work. Many of the high profile events during a school year have music at their core and there are correspondingly impressive standards expected and achieved at all levels.

Choosing the right school for your child is one of the most important decisions a family makes. At The Hall, we believe parents should be able to do so with clarity, confidence and trust.

They offer an objective snapshot of school life, grounded in evidence gathered through close observation, discussion and review. The Hall was last inspected by the Independent Schools Inspectorate (ISI) in April 2024.
We are proud of what our ISI report says about our community and we invite you to explore more below.

Partnerships with Primary Schools
The Hall is firmly committed to ensuring that the school and its teachers, parents and pupils play an integral role in the local community through educational partnerships and other schools and charitable organisations. As one of North London’s leading preparatory schools, we believe deeply in the responsibility to share our expertise, facilities, and opportunities in ways that create meaningful and lasting impact beyond our own community.
Our partnerships are ambitious, practical and long-term. Working closely with six local maintained primary schools, we collaborate to widen access, raise aspiration and enrich educational outcomes for hundreds of children each year.
Led by our Community Partnership Manager, our work is shaped by listening carefully to our partner schools and responding to genuine need through sustained collaboration.
Our Partnership Programmes
Saturday Club
Our flagship STEAM enrichment programme
Now in its ninth year, Saturday Club remains The Hall’s most established and impactful partnership initiative.
Developed alongside local headteachers, the programme was created to address the lack of access many children face to high-quality enrichment opportunities outside the classroom – particularly within STEAM subjects.
Each year, 55 pupils from Years 5 and 6 across our partner schools and The Winchester Project participate in 13 immersive sessions at The Hall. Activities include:
The programme cultivates confidence, curiosity and ambition, while helping pupils understand the real-world relevance of their learning.
Partner schools consistently report:
Several participants have successfully progressed to leading state and independent secondary schools, including Highgate, Channing, South Hampstead High School, UCS, and The Henrietta Barnett School, with a number supported through bursary and scholarship application processes.
A particularly powerful aspect of the programme is its culture of mentorship. Hall alumni and former Saturday Club participants return as volunteers and role models, helping to inspire the next generation.

The focus extends far beyond reading alone. Pupils develop oracy, comprehension, and critical-thinking skills while growing in confidence as communicators.

The Hall is a community dedicated to nurturing keen minds and generous hearts from ages 4-13. I invite you to visit us, experience our vibrant atmosphere, and discover for yourself what makes The Hall such an exceptional place for a boy to find his stride.

Drama
Drama is considered an important subject at The Hall, enabling students to grow in confidence, develop communication skills and creatively express their ideas. It is taught through the curriculum in the Junior School and as a discrete subject from Year 4 upwards. Dramatic play is recognised as essential to the child’s well-being, fostering the development of self in relation to others and the world about them.
Weekly lessons offer an exploration of various theatrical techniques and genres, from Mime and Mask to Narrative theatre, Ancient Greek theatre, Melodrama, Physical Theatre, and script work. Students are supported to develop an expressive use of voice and movement, but also to grow personally as there is a focus on developing empathy and cooperation with others.
Beyond the classroom, students benefit from an array of exciting opportunities. A weekly after-school Drama Club in the Senior School fosters continued learning and creative collaboration. Year 8 boys take part in Physical Theatre workshops with the renowned Frantic Assembly, while in Years 5 to 7 students enjoy workshops with West End dancers and choreographers, professional actors and puppeteers.
Highlighting teamwork, students in Year 7 and 8 engage in a yearly ‘Play in a Day’ Shakespeare workshop, culminating in performances of plays such as ‘A Midsummer Night’s Dream’, ‘Hamlet’ and ‘The Tempest’.
The department proudly stages a Senior School play each year, featuring productions such as ‘The Government Inspector’, ‘Hamlet’, and ‘The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time’. Students are involved not only on stage but also in operating lights, sound, and backstage support, gaining valuable experience in all aspects of theatre production.
The School has a good relationship with neighbouring Central School of Speech and Drama. In recent years MA Drama students have supported productions at the school as voice coaches and prop makers.
Over the years it has become clear that Drama at The Hall has inspired students to explore the subject further not only in their next schools but in their adult careers.

Music Information
Through largely practical activities in class lessons, boys have the opportunity to develop an enjoyment and appreciation of a wide range of music. They are encouraged and enthused to participate in musical activities and are able to improve their social skills and understanding through shared experience. They can explore their imagination, creativity, sensitivity and self-confidence as independent and self-motivated musicians, and they can expand their aesthetic awareness of music, history and culture.
The instrumental programme begins in the Junior School, where boys have the opportunity to become pianists or string players, as well as learning the recorder. They also begin to experience ensemble music making through the choir, the string group and the recorder group. In the Middle School and Senior Schools boys have access to lessons in a wide range of instruments and there are many opportunities to sing in choirs and play in orchestras, bands, chamber music groups and specialist ensembles. A supporting calendar of concerts, competitions, workshops and exams allows each individual to develop at their own pace and pursue their own musical interests.
A number of boys go on to win musical awards at top London day schools and national boarding schools, where competition is fierce and standards are extremely high. Whilst these pinnacles of achievement are to be celebrated, it is most important that boys at The Hall are encouraged to gain a life-long love and respect for the music that they experience, create and discover in the wider world.

Music School Staff
Luisa’s musical education began as a music scholar at Wells Cathedral School, Somerset. She went on to study at The Guildhall School of Music receiving a BMus (hons) and Post Graduate Diploma in Orchestral Playing. She was the winner of the college woodwind prize and was awarded a Junior Fellowship at the school in 2006.
Luisa was awarded an English Speaking Union Scholarship to study at Yale School of Music, USA, and a year later, the Banff Arts Centre Canada.
Luisa has performed throughout the UK and abroad with professional orchestras, chamber groups, and as a concerto soloist. Alongside her performing, she has always been actively involved in music education. She was previously Head of Woodwind and Percussion at Solihull School, and is delighted to be back at The Hall in its unique and thriving music department.
Martyn Kaine has been teaching at The Hall since 2000 alongside his freelance performance career; He has worked with many artists including Amy Winehouse, Joss Stone, Jamie Cullum, Nitin Sawnhney, Geowulf and Tony Visconti as well as the L.S.O and Metropole orchestras. He also writes, performs and records music for various film, T.V and radio shows commissioned by Universal Pictures, the BBC and Sky. He can often be found down at London’s Ronnie Scotts where he and some friends have performed monthly for the past 18 years as part Soul Family Sundays.
Martyn trained in music at Leeds College of Music, twice winning the drum kit prize, before completing a post grad at the Guildhall School of Music and Drama.
His various roles at The Hall include teaching Music Production and Drums/Percussion lessons one to one, as well as classroom based Music Technology lessons. He runs a percussion ensemble and assists in the Training and Concert Bands. Other roles include producing the Hall School Radio Podcast and various video content for the school.
Michael has spent much of his musical career immersed in both choral and church music, freelance performance, and music education. He has a long association with Trinity Laban London (formally Trinity College of Music), as a student and member of staff, both at the Senior and Junior Departments. As church musician he studied the organ with Dr Harry Gabb CVO and has been Director of Music and Organist at several churches in London (and Surrey). In September he became Director of Music as St Margaret’s Church, Putney having previously been the Cathedral Organist (Director of Music) at Holy Trinity Cathedral, Gibraltar. He has a wide range of choral conducting experience from children’s opera to youth choirs, including directing many school choirs, notably the boys’ choir, The Junior College Singers, from King’s College School, Wimbledon. Additionally, he has conducted many adult chamber choirs and is particularly known for his work with the Epsom Chamber Choir (PRS Award Winners), with whom he gave numerous first performances and produced several recordings. Having been Director of Music at several leading schools, including the choir school for King’s College, Cambridge, his work in education continues to be varied and now he divides his time between freelance work and his teaching commitments.
Ensemble Staff and Visiting Music Teachers (Self-Employed)
Hannah Biss is a violin and viola teacher specialising in the Suzuki method. Having completed a two-year specialist string-teaching PGCE at the Manchester Royal Northern College of Music in 1998 – which also gave her invaluable training and experience in Dalcroze and Kodaly teaching — Hannah completed the five-year Suzuki training in 2004. Since then, she has built her private teaching practice around Barnet, where she is based. Hannah enjoys teaching and coaching orchestras at both The Hall and Westminster School. She is currently Chair of the Trustees for the British Suzuki Institute.
Joss has some thirty years of teaching experience. Her pupils regularly achieve success, gaining music scholarships to study at some of London’s most prestigious schools, and winning prizes in various competitions. She runs several flute choirs, in and around London, and is in demand as a guest conductor with various others around the country. Joss delivers an annual residential course, for adults, at Benslow Music Trust in Hitchin, entitled, The Complete Flautist. At the age of thirteen, Joss made her London solo debut playing a concerto with The London Symphony Orchestra and was a scholar at The Royal College of Music followed by further studies at The Guildhall School of Music and Drama. Her flute playing has taken her all over the world as a soloist, an orchestral and chamber musician, a pit player in the West End and as an educator.
Sheida began learning the cello at the age of four and her teachers have included Joan Dickson, Florence Hooton, David Strange and Stefan Popov. She graduated with first-class honours from the Guildhall School of Music, then completed a year of study at the Hochschule für Musik in Cologne with Maria Kliegel and a Master of Music at the Eastman School of Music, USA (Steven Doane). As a chamber musician Sheida has performed abroad and in the BBC Martinu and Spitalfields Festivals in London. Recent performances include in the Purcell Room, St. John’s Smith Square, St. James’s Piccadilly, the National Portrait Gallery and on BBC Radio 3’s “In Tune”. Alongside her performing career, Sheida teaches for the charity Music Masters, and at the junior department of the Guildhall School of Music and Drama. Inspired by her love of chamber music, the children she teaches and with the encouragement of her own teachers and fellow musicians, Sheida set up Cellos/Strings Rock! courses in 2008. Sheida previously taught at the Greycoat Hospital School and at specialist string schemes such as Stringwise, Musicale, the Royal Academy of Music Junior Department and the Alexander Music School in Spain. At the City of London School for Girls and South Hampstead High School she established cello ensembles using her own arrangements of popular and classical music. She aims to encourage the development of group skills, which are essential elements of all string-players’ futures. Paying special attention to listening and rhythm, these sessions compliment what has been learned in individual lessons and provide a fun context in which these skills can evolve. Sheida is a member of both the Incorporated Society of Musicians and the European String Teachers Association.
Claire Duncan began playing the cornet at the age of 8. She spent her school days competing with contesting brass bands and playing with The National Youth Orchestra of Great Britain. At the age of 18, she was awarded a scholarship to The Guildhall School of Music and Drama, where she won the prestigious brass prize in her final year and performed with the European Community Youth Orchestra. Her main hobby is competing in various endurance sports such as Ironman triathlons and numerous marathons, including five London marathons. She has also cycled from John O’ Groats to Land’s End, raced 24-hour time trials and swum the English Channel.
Clare Hoskins read music at Trinity College, Cambridge, where she was a choral exhibitioner. Having then trained and worked as a primary school teacher, she left teaching to become a post-graduate student at the Royal Academy of Music, where she studied the oboe with Tess Miller and the cor anglais with Christine Pendrill for two years. Clare has worked extensively as a freelance player, including many years with Glyndebourne Touring Opera, Garsington Opera, and the Brighton Philharmonic Orchestra, as well as performing as an extra player with English National Opera, the orchestra of the Royal Opera House, the BBC Concert Orchestra, the Royal Philharmonic Orchestra, City of London Sinfonia, the London Mozart Players and the City of Birmingham Symphony Orchestra. Clare still works in education, teaching for Camden and Haringey Music Services and taking part in music workshops and outreach projects for orchestras with which she plays, and for Create Arts, a charity which aims to transform the lives of disadvantaged people through the creative arts.
Shelley Levy graduated from the University of Cape Town. She was awarded a prestigious Swiss government scholarship to study at the Geneva Conservatoire (‘Premiere Prix de Virtuosité’) before continuing at the Guildhall School of Music and Drama in London. Her teachers have included Oliver De Groote, Thomas Friedli, Walter Boeykens, Thea King and Michael Whight. She won the Oudemeester Competition for Wind Instruments, the Natal 75th Anniversary Prize for Orchestral Instruments and the wind category of the ATKV Forte Competition in South Africa and was a woodwind finalist in the Royal Overseas League Competition in London. As an orchestral freelancer she has played with the Cape Town Symphony Orchestra, Royal Philharmonic Orchestra and BBC Scottish Symphony Orchestra, amongst others. She has given numerous solo and chamber music concerts in South Africa, Europe and Canada, also giving concerto performances with all the major symphony orchestras in South Africa and chamber concerts at the Demetria Festival and Sani International Festival in Greece. Her UK performances include concerts in the Barbican and the Royal Albert Hall. She has been broadcast by BBC Radio 3 with Leto Ensemble. Shelley has recently released a CD of all Hans Gal’s works for clarinet and string on Toccata Classics record label, which featured in Gramophone magazine with a glowing review. Shelley teaches at Camden School for Girls and Camden Music Centre. She has also given masterclasses at Memorial University of Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada.
Jan Matthews has been teaching the violin at The Hall since 1989. She gives individual lessons to boys from Year 1 to Year 8, she coaches a number of string ensembles, and she directs the Middle School Orchestra. She has taught the violin at Arnold House School and also for the London boroughs of Camden, Hackney and Westminster. She leads and jointly manages The Oberon String Quartet: www.oberonquartet.co.uk.
Michiko was born in Japan, but has been living in the UK since 1994. She began playing the violin at the age of three with a Suzuki method teacher in Sendai. This early experience has significantly influenced her development as a music teacher, and she is now a fully accredited Suzuki violin teacher.
Michiko studied at the Royal Academy of Music in London, where she completed both an undergraduate degree and a postgraduate diploma in Violin Performance. On graduation, she also received the Music in the Community Award for her outreach work in schools. Her strong interest in children’s musical education has inspired her to explore and develop multiple teaching styles and methods, allowing her to identify the most effective strategies for helping her students to reach their full potential. A key aspect of her approach involves actively engaging and supporting the parents in the learning process.
Michiko combines her teaching with a freelance performing career. She regularly performs with many orchestras and chamber groups, as well as giving solo recitals across the UK and Japan.
Jamie O’Donnell has been working as a performer and educator since attending the Guildhall School of music and Drama in 1992. As an alto saxophonist and a prolific composer, Jamie has toured with many bands including the Pasadena roof Orchestra and the Gwilym Simcock Quintet. Jamie has taught jazz around the world for the International association of music in International schools and is a founder member of the Paradise Festival, Cyprus. His own group is currently touring, performing a tribute to the great bebop saxophonist, Phil Woods.
Ben Reynolds has enjoyed being part of the teaching team at The Hall since 2001. Alongside his one-to-one tuition, he also conducts and arranges music for three percussion ensembles which perform regularly in the school concerts and jazz evenings. Outside of school life, he is a percussionist performing in theatres and jazz clubs, as well as for radio and television around the United Kingdom and abroad. He is also a founder member and composer in the comedy/music group ‘The Horne Section’, which has had three Radio 4 series and has won several awards.
John Ward’s association with The Hall began in 2006 when he joined the Music Department as a singing teacher. In addition to his teaching work here, he has also played an active role in the Chapel Choir. He also teaches singing at Highgate School. When not teaching, he enjoys a busy and varied career as a freelance singer, working with the BBC Singers, The King’s Consort and Metro Voices, among others. He is also the bass lay clerk at Chelsea Old Church. Recent projects have included a tour to Singapore with the BBC Singers and singing on the film soundtracks of Guardians of the Galaxy and How to Train Your Dragon 2.
Ryan Williams completed a Bachelor of Music degree at the University of Exeter and went on to study Master of Music degree at the Guildhall School of Music and Drama in Jazz Performance. Since graduating, Ryan has led a busy freelance career across live performance, television and radio. Ryan had worked in a wide variety of musical settings having performed and recorded with many diverse artists including Andreya Triana, Then Jerico, Martha High and The Horne Section. Ryan also teaches at The Godolphin & Latymer School alongside working as an examiner for Rockschool.

Serene Koh holds an Artist Diploma and Masters with Distinction at the Guildhall School of Music and Drama where she studied with Martin Roscoe and Ronan O’hora, and was a scholarship recipient of The Eduard and Marianna Loeser Award. She currently teaches at Godolphin and Latymer School, The Hall School, and Norland Place School. Teaching is her focus and has been very inspiration

Our Governors
Governance at The Hall
The Hall is set up as an educational charity, The Hall School Charitable Trust, operating differently from public charities. Governors are similar to non-executive Directors and serve the school on a voluntary basis. The composition of the Hall’s Board reflects the world in which the school operates, with each Governor offering specific skills and expertise in an area, which is, or could be, of importance to The Hall.
In The Hall’s case, the largest skill set on the Board reflects the importance of – and emphasis on – our core ‘business’ of education. We are lucky enough to have the current Head of St Paul’s among our number. On the professional side, we have governors with accountancy skills, with investment experience, with legal knowledge (a solicitor and a barrister). Since we need to pay proper attention to our buildings and grounds we have a surveyor and property expert on the Board and recently we have recruited a leading PR consultant whose guidance is valuable in helping us to co-exist peacefully with our neighbours. Several of these Governors are current parents, past parents or former pupils and a representative of the Mercers’ Company, forming a link, which allows the school access to the broad knowledge and experience of the Company’s education committee. Together the Governors are a team that works together harmoniously for the good of the school.
So what do Governors do? Firstly they are the guardians of standards within the school. In brief summary, they must ensure that pupils are given the best possible, broad education in surroundings that are safe, conducive to learning and fit for purpose. In addition, they must ensure the financial health and well being of the school and, together with the school’s senior managers, must plan strategically for the future. The structure of the Governing Body and the schedule of meetings must be organised to support these and many other responsibilities.
There is a policy for Governance and among other things, this dictates a Governor’s term of office. This ensures both continuity and rotation; the Governing body is refreshed by seeking new recruits who are put forward by a Nominations Committee to fill specific gaps in order to retain a well-balanced Board with a broad spread of expertise. As a Board, we review our own performance on an annual basis.
The Hall School traces its roots back to 1889 when the Reverend Francis Wrottesley set up his own school, primarily to educate his own growing family of boys. He took in other paying pupils and so the Belsize School for Boys was born. He sold it in 1898 to the Reverend Douglas Marshall when pupil numbers had sunk to 13.
The Hall School Charitable Trust is registered at 23 Crossfield Road, Hampstead, London, NW3 4NU.

Curriculum Overview
We provide a multifaceted and broad curriculum in which academic, creative, physical, social, moral and spiritual elements are intrinsic and important parts. Through its delivery, we aim to support the boys in:
It is a continual great pleasure for those of us teaching here to help every boy work hard to fulfil his potential; we set high, challenging standards for all. The beauty of learning in an independent school, The Hall included, is that we are free from working within the frameworks prescribed for schools in the state-maintained sector. That said, much of what our boys learn is closely aligned to the schemes of work set out in the National Curriculum; we do our best to shape our programme to suit our needs however, thus ensuring it is fit for our purpose. At The Hall, the school day is busy and full, yet plenty of boys still find the time and energy to enjoy taking part in our extra-curricular activities too.
We also understand that our boys learn best in different ways. We, therefore, take advantage of a number of varied learning environments, through which the broad, balanced and relevant curriculum is delivered; plenty of learning happens in lessons of course, but also when our boys are out at Games, playing in concerts, acting in plays, on school trips here in the UK or abroad, as well as when they are completing tasks on their own at home in the evenings. Schemes of work are designed to provide plenty of scope for boys to tackle a range of tasks and activities that best match the breadth and depth of their abilities and then extend them. These schemes are reviewed annually.
Senior schools to which we send our boys are increasingly making decisions about the entry at 11+ when our boys are still in Year 6 or 7. We, therefore, prepare them for a range of senior schools’ pre-entry assessments so the boys can confidently meet these challenges, as well as those of the different school entrance frameworks taken at Year 8.
Growing into responsible, kind and happy adults.
Middle and Senior School Curriculums
Our curriculum is effectively planned around specific learning objectives for every subject area within each year group. The subjects taught across the Middle and Senior Schools encompass:
English | French
Maths | Science
Geography | History
Classics (Latin from Year 5)
TPR (Theology, Philosophy & Religion)
Music | Drama
Art & 3D Studies
Design & Technology
Computing | PE & Games
Life Skills
Digital Learning
The school is committed to developing a range of digital learning resources and providing a variety of technological opportunities for our pupils.
As intelligent and discerning learners with the capacity and appetite to learn from a variety of sources and situations, the boys navigate through a curriculum that enables them to acquire appropriate skills and dispositions in relation to using technology and digital learning resources. We want our pupils not just to use the latest technology and resources skilfully but also to create content and to experience working collaboratively becoming competent ‘digital citizens’, who easily and seamlessly integrate their technology skills across all learning areas.We embrace the concept of anytime, anyplace and anywhere learning while also allowing for the personalisation of the learning experience for each pupil. A good learning platform is therefore essential for pupils and staff; currently, we use the Firefly platform that allows teachers to celebrate students’ work, upload educational resources and create an online space that can be accessed from home and school. Parents also have the opportunity to discuss their views and listen to recent developments during the Parent Technology forums that take place once a term.Boys in the Senior School enjoy the opportunity to bring in their own devices from home. This allows for easy access to a wealth of resources on our learning platform and collaborative learning, including shared resources using Office 365 applications.
Spiritual, Moral, Social and Cultural Learning
Hall boys begin their exploration of spiritual, moral, social and cultural learning early, whilst still in the Junior School. Articulated in our key values, reflected in our pastoral system and codes of conduct as well as in the curriculum and co-curricular activities, we support and nurture boys by building their character so that they may show initiative, seek meaning and purpose, explore the mysteries of life and be creative and inventive.
Mutual respect and tolerance are at the core of school life; boys learn to treat each other and staff with great respect from the moment they arrive at the Junior School. We cherish being a multi-cultural school with families from a range of backgrounds and cultures, and we encourage and enhance the boys’ understanding of their place in a wider community by giving them opportunities to experience diversity and by rejecting discrimination based on difference.Assemblies, conference days, discussions and learning in class, all promote and effectively prepare the boys for ‘opportunities, responsibilities and experiences of life in British society’.
Our house system, the School Council and Eco-School meetings promote student voices and opportunities for boys to share their experiences and opinions in a safe environment. Boys have input with regard to the food they eat, after-school activity options and more significant eco issues, such as how the school deals with its waste. Pupil questionnaires and interviews are also frequently conducted to gauge opinion. The active participation of all our boys in these forums helps to sow the seeds for a more sophisticated understanding of democracy in the future and of society’s shared and agreed values.
Boys will encounter rules and laws throughout their entire lives. We want our pupils to understand that whether these laws govern the class, the school, the community or the country, they are set for good reasons and must be adhered to. This understanding of the importance of rules is consistently reinforced through assemblies and the curriculum by staff throughout the school. The involvement of boys in the creation of the school rules helps them to understand the reasons behind them and the consequences if they are broken. Through enquiry in our Life Skills curriculum and the wider curriculum, we allow an opportunity to debate and discuss the reasons for laws so that boys can recognise the importance of these for their own protection. Throughout the year, we welcome visits from members of the wider community, including police, politicians, religious members, war veterans, the fire brigade and many more, whose clear explanations and real-life stories emphasise the importance of the rule of law.

Register for 4+ Reception Entry
Starting school is an important and exciting milestone for both children and their families.
The Hall admits approximately 60 boys into Reception each September. Playdate assessments for these places take place during January and February in the year of entry.
We encourage families to attend one of our regular Open Mornings or Open Evenings, or to arrange a private tour during term time to see The Hall in action and meet members of our school community.
View upcoming Open Events and book a tour
Register for 4+ Entry
By registering, you are formally applying for a place in Reception and your son will be invited to participate in the 4+ assessment process. Registration closes in November prior to the January/February playdate assessments. For Reception 2027 entry, the deadline to register is 2nd November 2026. We encourage families to register as early as possible.
The fee for a Reception‑year application is £180 (non‑refundable). Please use your son’s full name as the payment reference so we can match the payment with your form.
If you have any questions about registration or the admissions process, please contact our Registrar, Lucy Richards, who will be delighted to help: l.richards@hallschool.co.uk
Please download the Step-by-Step Guide to Admissions into Reception

Welcome to Admissions at The Hall
Welcome from the Registrar – Lucy Richards
Choosing the right school is such an important moment for any family and, at The Hall, we want that experience to feel calm, clear, and genuinely supportive. As the Registrar, I’m here to guide you through our admissions process – answering your questions, offering clarity where you need it, and helping you navigate each step with confidence.
The best way to understand what makes The Hall unique is to come and visit us. I warmly encourage you to book onto an Open Event or get in touch to arrange a personal tour – it’s the simplest way to get a real sense of how special our boys, our staff, and everyday life is here.
If you’d like to talk through entry points or the admissions process, please do get in touch. I’m always happy to help guide you through any aspect of your family’s journey.
Lucy RichardsRegistrar, The Hall
Phone: +44(0)7739061977Email: l.richards@hallschool.co.uk
